title: P.S.
full_review:
A lonely, thirtysomething academic gets a second shot at first love in "P.S." (Newmarket), a lightweight romantic comedy, which unfortunately is short on both romance and comedy.

Directed by Dylan Kidd, the modest Manhattan love story has all the elements of a good independent film, including a smart script and a top-notch ensemble, headed by Laura Linney, Marcia Gay Harden and Gabriel Byrne. Yet taken as a whole, the movie somehow adds up to less than the sum of its proficient parts.

Linney stars as Louise Harrington, a recently divorced admissions director at Columbia University's School of Fine Arts, who has settled into unfulfilled single-life solitude after the amicable breakup with her professorial husband, Peter (Byrne).

That all changes when she receives a graduate application from a talented young artist, F. Scott Feinstadt (Topher Grace), with almost the same name as her high school sweetheart -- and one true love -- who was tragically killed in a car crash while they were still teens. She sets up an interview and is further surprised to find that Scott bears an uncanny resemblance to her lost love. Could it be him? He even paints the same way. Within hours they embark on a torrid May-December affair.

Harden plays Louise's oversexed gal pal, Missy, who back in their high school days had stolen the original Scott from Louise and is now licking her lascivious chops at the prospect of a repeat performance with the doppelganger.

As directed by Kidd, the film, based on a novel of the same name by Helen Schulman, dwells tenderly on issues of longing, love and loneliness and midlife fears of unrealized dreams. But the moral and narrative ambiguity of the ending is less than satisfying and offers little insight into the characters, let alone the wider human condition.

While some viewers may find her almost instantaneous amorous overtures off-putting, Louise's sexual advances (handled with relative restraint) seem to be fueled more by loneliness than lust.

The best part of the film is the cast, topped by Linney, whose disarming natural charm and ability to effortlessly emote vulnerability elevate the movie above its overall mediocrity. Grace is equally good, imbuing his role with a delicate blend of self-satisfied smugness and insecurity. Harden sizzles, making the most of her limited screen time. Apart from one dramatically juicy scene where he confesses numerous past infidelities to his wife, Byrne is underused, as is Paul Rudd as Louise's recovering-addict brother.

In exploring the coincidences surrounding the two Scott characters, the movie skirts with mysticism, but never really commits one way or the other, seasoning its story with kismet and cul-de-sacs concerning soul transference and reincarnation that are left, for the most part, unresolved. And while the concept of soul migration stands in conflict with Catholic teachings about the afterlife, it has, as a plot device, been used to much better effect in such films as 1978's "Heaven Can Wait" and 1989's "Chances Are."

Due to a sexual encounter and a few implied encounters, as well as recurring rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
